newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan investors waking up to Africa.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan investors waking up to Africa.

text.p: You have to travel almost a whole day and a night to get to Johannesburg from Japan, even with a direct flight that was launched in April.
But Japan is finally waking up to the potential of the African continent, three years after Nelson Mandela was elected to head South Africa's first post-apartheid government.

"Japanese companies have started to invest in South Africa for expanding their market share there and in the neighbouring countries," said Kazuyoshi Kawaguchi, an official at the overseas planning division of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.
CARMAKERS LEAD THE PACK
Over the last several months, Japan's top car makers Toyota Motor Corp and Nissan Motor Co Ltd as well as tyre maker Bridgestone Corp have announced plans to move into South Africa.

Toyota is to pour in 446 million rand ($100 million) and Nissan 350 million rand to acquire a stake in local car manufacturers, while Bridgestone is to pay 290 million rand to take over a local tyre plant which once belonged to U.S. firm Firestone Inc.

According to Nissan, the South African car market, which saw vehicle sales of 380,000 units in 1996, is set to grow to 500,000 units by the year 2000. Nissan also hopes to boost exports throughout the continent from its base in South Africa.

Toyota, Nissan and Bridgestone were the first Japanese to join Johannesburg's list of major foreign investors but stand far behind others, such as Malaysian state-run Petroliam Nasional (Petronas) which is to spend two billion rand.
OTHERS HESISTANT TO FOLLOW

"Japanese companies seem to be not fully active in participating in unique opportunities for investment in South Africa and Southern Africa," said Brendon Roberts, economic counsellor of the South African embassy in Tokyo.
"It's clearly physical distance, coupled with psychological distance and lack of history (of conducting business in the continent)," Roberts added.
Official data show the African continent accounts for less than two percent of Japan's overall trade and investment, with South Africa comprising about half of the total.

"Unfortunately our eyes are on China, Asia and Latin America," said Hitoshi Suzuki, manager in charge of trade with Europe and Africa at trade house Nissho Iwai Corp. "That's where we see strong growth in the near future."
TRYING TO TURN THE TIDE
In an attempt to turn the tide, the South African government and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi signed an agreement in January to work together to promote Japanese direct investment to South Africa.

It plans a first round of seminars for possible investors in June when South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel visits Japan, and Johannesburg issued its second yen-denominated samurai bond on Tuesday.

"As South Africa's economy expands, purchasing power in neighbouring countries will also rise," Tokyo-Mitsubishi's Kawaguchi said. "South Africa's population is 40 million, but the region has some 140 million people."

Over the last three years, Japan's investment in Africa has increased, though from a very low level. Metal groups have rushed into South Africa to secure a supply of its natural resources, hand in hand with trading houses.
CAUTION AMONG METAL COMPANIES
"Imports of manufactured goods from South Africa are on the rise, particularly metal products," said Kotaro Kodama, official at the Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO).
"Japan is increasingly smelting and refining ores in South Africa for export to Japan and other Asian countries, instead of bringing ore to Japan."

Mitsui & Co Ltd, the most aggressive in Africa among Japanese trading houses, is involved not only in the move by Nissan, but has set up joint ventures in South Africa for distribution of ferrochrome and manganese alloys. Together with South Africa's Gencor Ltd and Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co Ltd, it is also conducting a feasibility study for building a 1.7-billion-rand zinc refinery in South Africa's Eastern Cape province.
"We will see more investment for mineral projects," said Shigeharu Sawai, a manager at Mitsui's overseas department.
"It's important to get our hands on non-ferrous metals because Eastern Asian demand will rise in line with their industrialisation," he said.
But many Japanese companies are reluctant to invest in other African countries which are in dire need of hard currency and technology transfer, even in the mining sector.
No Japanese name was found among bidders for Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM), though Japan relies on imports from that country to meet about 15 percent of its copper demand.
None seems to be dashing into the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, where the demise of former president Mobutu Sese Seko has opened new opportunities.

"There's a saying that 'capital is a coward'. It doesn't go where it seems slightly dangerous," said Mitsui's Sawai. "We won't be going to Zambia or Zaire. If at all, it will be together with South African mining groups. They say they know best about Africa."
